analytic.title: Transition-aware Real-Time Task Scheduling for Reconfigurable Embedded Systems

textClass.keywords: Dynamically reconfigurable systems and Real-time task scheduling

div.p: Due to increase in demand for reconfigurability in embedded systems, real-time task scheduling is challenged by non-negligible reconfiguration overheads. If such overheads are not considered, tasks may not be schedulable under given deadlines, and hence, affecting the quality of service. We introduce the problem of real-time periodic task scheduling under transition overhead on heterogeneous reconfigurable systems. We formulate the problem as a network flow problem and provide a mixed integer linear programming solution. We compare our proposed solution with optimal scheduling under maximum fixed transition overhead. We deployed our method on task scheduling for multiple communication protocols on reconfigurable FPGA-like systems. Results show that our proposed scheduling improves the task schedulability by 24.2% in comparison with non-preemptive EDF and by 17.5% in comparison with maximum-transition-overhead scheduling.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Scheduling in real-time embedded systems is mostly coupled with stringent constraints such as hardware resources, power, performance and hard deadline constraints. Many embedded system applications are not only computationally intensive but also require great amount of flexibility and configurability. Hence, the integration of runtime reconfiguration is becoming an unavoidable scheme in embedded systems. Flexibility and reconfigurability bring a new perspective to resource management and real-time task scheduling in such embedded systems. While configurations such as dynamic frequency/voltage scheduling [1,2,3] may not incur significant timing transition overhead, hardware reconfiguration in reconfigurable architectures (coarse-grained or fine-gained such as FPGAs), online co-processor updates, and reconfiguration of soft processors may incur non-negligible transition overhead during real-time scheduling in such systems. This paper focuses on transition-aware real-time task scheduling on reconfigurable embedded systems.

In such real-time task scheduling, multiple tasks are scheduled on multiple processing units similar to task scheduling on multiprocessors. However, the underlying system needs to be updated/reconfigured (partially/fully) between the executions of two consecutive tasks on a processing element if each requires a different configuration of the processor unit. In real-time task scheduling on reconfigurable embedded systems, preemptive scheduling is not applicable due to transition overhead both in terms of memory and delay overhead. The input to reconfigurable embedded systems are mostly streaming data (multimedia and communication systems), and hence, periodic task model has widely been used to model such recurring processes. In this paper, we tackle the problem of non-preemptive scheduling on real-time periodic tasks considering the transition overhead between the tasks. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to propose a non-preemptive real-time task scheduling in embedded systems with varying transition overhead between the tasks. While existing real-time scheduling algorithms can be adopted to include transition overhead as a constant (such as WCET), the solution to such scheduling can be very pessimistic and may lead to degradation in performance and quality of service of the system. We model the real-time task scheduling problem under transition overhead on multiple processing elements as to find disjoint routes in the graph representing the periodic tasks under their corresponding arrival times and deadlines. As a result, we formulate the problem as a class of network flow problem and present a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation of the problem, which enables us to extend the problem to various cases for real-time embedded systems such as delaying start time of the tasks or exploiting timing slack, as well as to include additional constraints such as heterogeneity of processing elements in embedded systems.

We deploy the proposed solution for real-time scheduling in time slot allocation for packet processing of multiple protocols implemented on FPGA-like reconfigurable hardware. For example, FPGA is reconfigured to support DSP processing for WCDMA (Wideband Code Division Multiple Access) after processing the packets for WiFi. Such reconfiguration takes orders of milliseconds. Exploiting such optimization makes MAC layer aware of reconfiguration overhead during packet scheduling without which, several time slots allocated for packet processing may not be used at the physical layer due to reconfiguration overhead. In experiments, we setup various time allocations of several protocols such as WiFi, WiMax (Worldwide Interoperability for Microwave Access), WCDMA, and GPRS (General Packet Radio Service). On average, our approach improves the task schedulability by 24.2% compared to adopted non-preemptive EDF (Earliest Deadline First) [4] and by 17.5% compared to optimal scheduling under maximum fixed transition overhead. On synthetic benchmarks, the proposed scheduler outperforms adopted EDF by 27.33% (on average) and scheduling with maximum transition overhead by 20.75% (on average) in terms of schedulability.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: There have been extensive studies in the literature on realtime task scheduling in embedded systems [2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]. In [2,3,5], scheduling with power, energy or thermal awareness is presented. Several research works focus on real-time task scheduling on reconfigurable FPGAs, but transition overhead is either ignored [6,7] or considered as a constant [8,9].

There are several works considering the non-preemptive task scheduling on single processor [4,10] and multiple processors [11,12]. But none of them consider the transition overhead between tasks. To the best of our knowledge this paper is the first paper considering this overhead.

div.head: III. TARGET PLATFORM
div.p: In this paper we target a heterogeneous platform consisting of several Processing Elements (PEs). These PEs can be a DSP processor, reconfigurable processors (soft processors), processors with reconfigurable coprocessors and/or memory, or a reconfigurable hardware (fine or coarse grained) (see Figure 1). For each PE, there is a reconfigurable part which is reconfigured/updated during the runtime. Based on the task scheduling timings, the reconfiguration manager forces the PEs to reconfigure appropriately.

We target real-time system for streaming applications such as multimedia applications and communication systems in which tasks are fully streaming (i.e. during the execution, tasks receive inputs and send outputs).

div.head: A. Interface Model
div.p: In our system model, there is no data dependency between the tasks but there is an input/output interface for streaming data being processed. This interface can be communication with a memory or a peripheral device like a wireless antenna. We consider two interface architectures in our model: (1) In dedicated Interface, each PE has dedicated input and output. Hence, PEs can run different tasks parallel to each other (Figure 2

div.head: B. Transition Overhead
div.p: Transition overhead is the time needed after ending the current task to start the next task. We model this transition overhead in three categories: 1) Fixed overhead: This type of overhead is a fixed overhead per task on all PEs. This is applicable to homogeneous PEs. We assume this overhead as a part of the execution time.

div.head: C. Input Tasks
div.p: We are given a set of non-preemptive periodic tasks (τ) with corresponding start time and deadline (Figure 1). The execution time of each task on each PE is known a priori. In addition, we assume that a transition overhead exists between the executions of two consecutive tasks on each PE as modeled above. Tasks are independent, i.e., the time a task is invoked depends only upon its period and not upon the invocation time of other task. There is no priority between the tasks.

div.head: D. Parameterized Inputs
div.p: In many streaming applications, some input parameters such as start time and input load are flexible and hence, could be deployed during real-time task scheduling.

div.head: 1) Delayed start time:
div.p: We can delay start time of some tasks in order to reduce the time overlap among different tasks. If the execution time of the tasks has less overlap, the tasks will have less competition during scheduling and more tasks are schedulable. However, we can delay each task instance as far as its finish time would not exceed the task period. In this parameterization, we do not change the start time of the periods, but only delaying the execution time of a task instance within its interval. The same delay applies to all the instances of a given periodic task (Figure 3-a).

2) Input load increase: In this case, we first schedule the tasks. After scheduling, if there was some slack time available, we will exploit the slack time and increase the input load which will result in increasing the throughput. Input load of all the instances of a task will increase with the same amount (Figure 3-b). . If all the PEs are identical, we refer to execution time as e i . The inter-task overhead between the tasks τ i and τ j on PE r is r ij s and task initiation overhead of task τ i on PE r is o i r . In order to increase performance, we allow idle times on each PE (if needed) even though some tasks are ready for execution (forbidden regions in [13]).

Given the period, the execution time and the relative deadline of each task, we compute the time window during which each instance of the tasks should start execution in order to finish their job before the deadline. We present each instance of the periodic tasks with a node in a directed graph and each node is associated with corresponding time window of the task. For simplicity, we now focus on task scheduling on one PE. Each edge in this graph represents the transition overhead between two consecutive tasks on a PE. Figure 4-a shows an example of two tasks in the graph. Fixed overheads and task initiation overheads are associated with the nodes. But intertask overheads are associated with the edges.

The path represents the order of the tasks scheduled on one PE. The longest path would provide the maximum number of tasks schedulable on a single PE.

On multiple PEs, we need to find multiple disjoint paths and cover all the nodes in order to provide a feasible schedule for all the task instances. This is the first effort to model the real-time scheduling problem under transition overhead as vehicle routing problem. We then present an MILP (mixed integer linear programming) solution for the proposed real-time scheduling problem. The proposed problem formulation targets the real-time scheduling problem under various constraints and conditions that we face in reconfigurable systems and streaming applications.

div.head: A. Synthetic benchmarks
div.p: We evaluated the performance of the proposed scheduling algorithm based on simulations. We implemented our MILPs using CPLEX and for comparison, we adopted non-preemptive EDF algorithm [4] to consider transition overhead. Although EDF is an online scheduling, we compared it with our optimal solution to show the deviation from optimal value if EDF is simply adopted. Table III shows the number of periodic sets and the number of PEs used in each experiment. For each case, we generated 5-6 different inputs. In each set we had considered both types of interface model (i.e. dedicated interface and shared interface). For all the benchmarks the P Total is equal to 60 and period of each task is chosen from the set {4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15}. We have three cases for deadline (i.e. D=P, D=P/2 and D=2P) and the execution time is a random number smaller than min(D,P). We applied the best effort objective to the inputs. In Table III, the schedulability (number of feasible task instances divided by total number of task instances) for different inputs using different scheduling methods are reported. On average, our proposed scheduler provides 20.75% and 27.33% improvement in comparison with EDF and maximum overhead scheduling respectively.

div.head: B. CASE STUDY: multiple communication protocol support on runtime reconfigurable FPGAs
div.p: In this paper, we target Software Defined Radio (SDR) [15] applications implemented on FPGA. Figure 6-a shows a SDR application with 3 protocols and 2 FPGAs. Multiple communication support is realized through runtime reconfiguration of FPGA devices. Base-station architecture of SDR is illustrated in Figure 6-b. Various non-time stringent data link layer protocols run in the software portion of the SDR platform, while the hardware portion implements the time stringent and computationally intensive modulation/demodulation (modem) functions. Since the topper layer is not time stringent, it is the job of our scheduler to schedule the protocols and make it time stringent for the lower layer. We deploy our scheduler for time slot allocation to protocols while considering transition delay overhead of underlying hardware. The protocols used in this application are WiFi, WiMax, GPRS and WCDMA. We chose Xilinx Virtex II as the target FPGA device. We have reconfiguration overhead between each pair of protocols and they are shown Table IV (numbers are milliseconds). In calculating these values we consider the common components between protocols, for example if we are transiting between two protocols and both of them are using FFT, then there is no need to configure this component on the FPGA because it is already configured on the FPGA. We have 8 scenarios in this case study. 6 scenarios have 3 protocols and 2 FPGAs and 2 of them have 4 protocols and 3 FPGAs. The first experiment is with the best effort objective. In Table V, the schedulability of each method for different scenarios are reported and the results show on average 24.2% and 17.5% improvement in comparison with adopted EDF and maximum overhead scheduling, respectively. Next simulation is minimizing the total transition overhead. Results are shown in Table VI. On average, the total transition overhead in EDF and in maximum overhead scheduling are 4 and 6 times greater transition overhead in our scheduling with parameterized inputs, respectively. However, EDF and maximum overhead scheduling were not even able to schedule all the tasks in some cases. Table VII shows time slots allocated to protocols WiFi and GPRS in our simulations (in msec). With parameterized input simulation, time slots allocated to WiFi increases in all the 8 scenarios. For GPRS protocol the original timing allocates two GPRS time slots (each GPRS time slot is 0.578ms) but with parameterized inputs, in some scenarios we were able to allocate 3 GPRS time slots. On average the time slot allocated to WiFi and GPRS increase 10.72% and 19.81% respectively. In addition to these improvements, Table V indicates that we gain 3% improvement in terms of schedulability using parameterized inputs. The time slots allocated to other protocols are unchanged.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presents a novel non-preemptive real-time task scheduling under transition overhead for reconfigurable embedded systems. We present an MILP formulation for the problem and applied our scheduling to time slot allocation for packet processing in system with multiple protocol support, realized by reconfigurable hardware at the physical layer. The results show 24.2% improvement in comparison with EDF and 17.5% in comparison with maximum overhead scheduling in soft real-time scheduling (best effort). As a future work we intend to develop an intuitive heuristic to tackle the problem efficiently.

By changing the ordering of the tasks on a specific PE, this overhead does not change. 3) Inter-task overhead: This type of overhead depends on PE and the current task as well as the next incoming task. The ordering of the tasks on a PE affects this overhead. Examples are partial reconfiguration overhead in reconfigurable hardware or instruction loading in a memory. Incorporating such transition overhead to real-time scheduling is our contribution in this work.
